He slipped quietly out through the wooden wall panelling, an evil smile on his cruel, wrinkled lips. The moon hid behind a cloud as he crept past the great projecting window, which displayed his coat of arms and that of his murdered wife in blue and gold. He drifted onwards like a wicked shadow, and even the darkness seemed to shrink from him. Once he stopped, thinking he had heard a call. But it was only a dog howling at the Red Farm, and he continued, muttering strange curses from the sixteenth century. Now and then he waved his rusty dagger in the midnight air. At last he came to the corner of the passage leading to unfortunate Washington's room. He paused there briefly. The wind tossed his long grey hair and twisted the dreadful burial sheet he wore into strange, distorted folds. Then the clock struck the quarter-hour, and he knew the moment had arrived. Chuckling to himself, he rounded the corner. Immediately he stumbled back with a pitiful cry of terror and covered his white face with his long, bony hands. Directly before him stood a horrible ghost, as still as a statue and as monstrous as something dreamed by a madman. Its bare head shone; its face was round, fat, and white. Hideous laughter seemed to have twisted its features into a permanent grin. Red beams streamed from its eyes, and its mouth was a deep, wide opening filled with fire. A dreadful garment like his own wrapped its enormous body in silent, snowy folds. On its chest hung a sign covered in strange, old-fashioned lettering. It seemed to record some shameful history, some catalogue of terrible sins and crimes. In its right hand it raised a broad, curved sword of shining steel.

Having never seen a ghost before, he was naturally terrified. After one more hurried glance at the dreadful figure, he ran back to his room, stumbling over his long burial sheet as he raced along the corridor. Finally he dropped the rusty dagger into the Minister's high leather boots, where the butler found it next morning. Safe inside his own room, he threw himself onto a small, simple bed and buried his face beneath the covers. Before long, though, the old Canterville courage returned, and he decided that once daylight came he would go and speak to the other ghost. So, just as the dawn began to touch the hills with silver, he headed back towards the place where he had first seen the terrifying figure. After all, he thought, two ghosts were better than one. With his new friend's help, he might be able to tackle the twins without danger to himself.

Mr. Podgers suddenly let go of Lord Arthur's right hand and grabbed his left. He bent so close to inspect it that the gold frames of his glasses almost touched the palm. For an instant his face turned into a white mask of horror. Then he regained his composure and looked up at Lady Windermere with a strained smile. ‘This is the hand of a charming young man.’

‘Naturally!’ Lady Windermere replied. ‘But will he make a charming husband? That's what I want to know.’

‘Every charming young man does,’ said Mr. Podgers.

‘I don't think husbands should be too captivating,’ Lady Jedburgh murmured thoughtfully. ‘It's so dangerous.’

‘My dear, they never are,’ Lady Windermere exclaimed. ‘But I want details. Nothing else interests me. What is going to happen to Lord Arthur?’

‘Well, sometime in the next few months Lord Arthur will take a voyage—’

‘Yes, of course, his honeymoon!’

‘And he will lose a relative.’

‘Surely not his sister?’ Lady Jedburgh asked in a distressed voice.

‘Certainly not,’ Mr. Podgers answered, waving away the suggestion. ‘Only a distant relative.’

‘Well, I'm terribly disappointed,’ said Lady Windermere. ‘I have absolutely nothing to tell Sybil tomorrow. Nobody bothers about distant relatives these days. They fell out of fashion years ago. Still, I suppose she should have a black silk dress ready. It will always do for church, you know. Now let's go to supper. I'm sure they've eaten everything, but there may be some hot soup left. François once made excellent soup, but politics have him so worked up these days that I never quite know what to expect from him. I do wish General Boulanger would be quiet. Duchess, you must be tired?’

‘Not at all, dear Gladys,’ replied the Duchess, waddling towards the door. ‘I've enjoyed myself enormously, and the podiatrist—I mean, the palm reader—is most interesting. Flora, where's my tortoiseshell fan? Oh, Sir Thomas, thank you so much. And my lace shawl, Flora? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, how very kind.’ The good creature eventually made it downstairs, dropping her perfume bottle only twice.

Throughout all this, Lord Arthur Savile had stood beside the fireplace, still gripped by the same dread, the same sickening certainty that something terrible was approaching. He gave his sister a sad smile as she swept past on Lord Plymdale's arm, lovely in pink brocade and pearls. He scarcely heard Lady Windermere calling him to come with her. His thoughts were with Sybil Merton, and the possibility that anything might separate them brought tears to his eyes.

Clearing things up with Mr. Knightley had given Emma great pleasure. It was one of the happy memories of the ball that she enjoyed as she walked about the lawn the next morning. She was delighted that they now understood each other's views about the Eltons, and that they thought so much alike about both husband and wife. His praise of Harriet, and his willingness to admit her merits, pleased Emma especially. For a few minutes the Eltons' rudeness had threatened to spoil the rest of her evening. Instead, it had led to some of its happiest moments. She hoped it would bring another benefit: an end to Harriet's infatuation. The way Harriet had spoken about the incident before they left the ballroom gave Emma good reason for hope. Her eyes seemed suddenly to have opened. She could now see that Mr. Elton was not the exceptional man she had imagined. The fever had passed, and Emma hardly feared that any harmful show of politeness would set Harriet's heart racing again. She could trust the Eltons' hostility to provide whatever further lessons Harriet needed through their deliberate neglect. With Harriet thinking sensibly, Frank Churchill only moderately in love, and Mr. Knightley unwilling to quarrel with her, what a happy summer Emma could expect!

She would not see Frank Churchill that morning. He had told her he could not enjoy a visit to Hartfield, since he needed to reach home by noon. She felt no disappointment.

Having considered these matters and settled everything to her satisfaction, she was just turning towards the house. Her refreshed spirits had prepared her for the demands of the two little boys and their grandfather. Then the great iron carriage gate opened, and two people came in whom she could hardly have expected to see together: Frank Churchill, with Harriet leaning on his arm. It really was Harriet! Emma needed only a moment to realize that something unusual had happened. Harriet was pale and frightened, and Frank was trying to comfort her. The iron gates were less than twenty yards from the front door, so all three soon reached the hall. Harriet immediately sank into a chair and fainted.

A young woman who faints must be brought round; questions need answers, and surprises need explanations. Such events are exciting, but their suspense cannot continue for long. Within a few minutes Emma knew the whole story.

Miss Smith and Miss Bickerton, another pupil who boarded as part of Mrs. Goddard's household, had gone out walking together. Miss Bickerton had also attended the ball. They had chosen the Richmond road, which seemed busy enough to be safe but had brought them a fright. About half a mile beyond Highbury, the road took a sharp turn. Elm trees cast deep shade on either side, and for quite a distance it was very secluded. The young women had walked some way along this stretch when they suddenly noticed a group of Gypsies a short distance ahead, on a wider patch of grass beside the road.
